Reflexive pronouns are pronounced together with the verb, without a pause: “mătrezesc”, “tespeli”, “seîmbracă”.
“duș”, “oraș”: the final “ș” is clearly heard, like “sh”.
In “să meargă”, “să facă”, the final “ă” is short and weak, but audible. It makes the difference between “merge” (he goes) and “meargă” (that he go).
Consonant clusters are pronounced without an extra vowel: “grăbi” (not “gu-răbi”), “trezi”, “scrie”.

Many verbs describing a daily routine are reflexive: the action turns back onto the person. In the dictionary they appear with “se”: a se trezi, a se spăla. The reflexive pronoun changes with the person and goes before the verb.
What time do you wake up?
We go to bed at eleven.
Some verbs are reflexive in Romanian but not in other languages: “mă grăbesc” (I hurry), “mă uit” (I look), “mă bucur” (I am glad).
2. -e verbs: a merge, a face, a scrie
As with -esc verbs, in -e verbs “eu” and “ei” have the same form: “eu merg” (I go), “ei merg” (they go).
“A merge” also means “to work, to function”: “Ceasul nu merge.” (The clock doesn’t work.) And “Merge!” = It’s fine! It works.
3. Vreau să…, pot să…, trebuie să…

When two verbs follow each other, the second one usually comes after “să”. This is the form called the subjunctive, one of the most used forms in Romanian. Instead of an infinitive (“I want to go”), Romanian says “vreau să merg”.
I don’t want to eat now.
Good news: for “eu, tu, noi, voi”, the form after “să” is exactly the same as the present: “să merg, să mergi, să mergem, să mergeți”.
“Trebuie” has the same form for all persons: “eu trebuie să plec” (I must leave), “tu trebuie să pleci” (you must leave), “ei trebuie să plece” (they must leave).
In the third person (el, ea, ei, ele), the form after “să” changes. The general rule: the ending -ă becomes -e, and -e / -ește becomes -ă / -ească.
Mițu wants to go to the office.
Radu has to play on Friday.
“A fi” has special forms after “să”: să fiu, să fii, să fie, să fim, să fiți, să fie. “Vreau să fiu odihnită.” (I want to be rested.)
To tell things in order: “mai întâi” (first), “apoi” (then), “după aceea” (after that), “la sfârșit” (at the end). “Mai întâi mă spăl, apoi mă îmbrac.” (First I wash, then I get dressed.)

People have a problem: they are always in a hurry. I, Mițu, am never in a hurry. I want to tell you about my perfect day.
I wake up at five, together with Mrs Pop. I don’t get up. Why should I get up? Her bed is warm.
At six, Mrs Pop gets up and makes coffee. Then I get up too and wash myself. I wash very thoroughly: my paws, my ears, my tail. It takes twenty minutes. A tomcat must be elegant.
At seven, Nora wakes up and rushes. She has a shower, gets dressed, drinks her coffee standing up. I watch her and don’t understand. Why drink coffee standing up when there are chairs?
Then Nora leaves. Sometimes I want to go with her, but I can’t. The door closes too quickly.
At eight I eat. At nine I sleep in the armchair. At twelve I sleep in the sun, on the windowsill. At three I sleep on Nora’s bed, because it smells of her.
In the evening, everyone comes home. Mrs Pop cooks, Nora draws, and Radu sometimes plays the violin. Then I hide under the bed.
On Friday, Radu has a big concert. Mrs Pop and Nora want to go. I can’t go, but never mind.
When they leave for the concert, the flat is all mine. And that, my dears, is the best music.

“odată cu” = at the same time as
